theme: The LORD is my light and my salvation
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 27. It begins with confident trust and ends with patient waiting. Notice how fear and faith sit side by side.
settingTheScene: Psalm 27 is a psalm of David. The first half (vv. 1-6) is bold, an army encamped around him and his heart unafraid. The second half (vv. 7-14) is a plea, almost trembling, for God to hear. Some think it is two psalms joined, but the effect is true to life: courage in the morning, anxiety in the evening, and both brought to God. It comes in the plan beside Luke’s teaching on fear and trust.
observation: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (v. 1).
“The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (v. 1).
“Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear” (v. 3).
“One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (v. 4).
“You have said, Seek my face. My heart says to you, Your face, LORD, do I seek” (v. 8).
“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in” (v. 10).
“I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living!” (v. 13).
“Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!” (v. 14).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with three names for God: light, salvation, stronghold. Light shows the way and drives out darkness. Salvation delivers. A stronghold protects. With these three, David asks, “Whom shall I fear?” The questions are not worried. They expect the answer, “No one.”

Then he lists the threats: evildoers who devour, an army, war. And still: “In this I will be confident.” His confidence rests on one desire: “One thing have I asked of the LORD.” Out of all the things he could ask, he asks for God’s presence. He wants to dwell in the house of the LORD, gaze on his beauty, and inquire in his temple. In the day of trouble, God will hide him in his shelter and set him high on a rock. Then he will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy.

At verse 7 the tone shifts. “Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me!” The confident man is also a man in need. He remembers God’s invitation, “Seek my face,” and answers with the same words. He asks God not to hide his face, not to cast him off. Even if his father and mother forsake him, the LORD will take him in.

He asks to be taught God’s way and led on a level path, and he asks to be saved from false witnesses. Then verse 13 is the hinge: “I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living!” He does not wait for heaven to see God’s goodness. It will come here.

The last verse is an exhortation to himself and to us: wait. Be strong. Take courage. Wait. Waiting is not passive but active trust. In Luke, Jesus said, “Fear not, little flock.” David and Jesus say the same thing. The Lord is light, and there is nothing to fear in his presence.
connection: Psalm 23 shares the theme of God’s presence in danger. Psalm 42 and 63 share the thirst for God. Isaiah 60:1 and John 8:12 speak of the light. Matthew 6:33 says to seek first the kingdom. 2 Corinthians 4:6 says God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. Romans 8:31 asks, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Isaiah 40:31 promises renewed strength to those who wait on the LORD.
application:
Say verse 1 aloud, then name the thing you are most afraid of right now and say “Whom shall I fear?”

Write down your “one thing” from verse 4. What do you most want from God?

Choose something to wait on in prayer, and wait with courage.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you fear, and say, “The LORD is my light and my salvation.”
Ask him for the one thing: to dwell with him and see his beauty.
Tell him you wait for him.
